scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

prediction.raw: This is a **1 (not AITA)**—but with important nuances to consider. Here’s why: ### **Why It’s Not AITA:** 1. **Your Money, Your Rules**: You’ve worked hard to save for *your* future vacation, and it’s yours to use as you see fit. You’re not obligated to loan it to your brother, especially since he’s unreliable with money and hasn’t contributed to his own savings. 2. **Different Priorities**: Your goal is a post-graduation trip, while his is a mid-year vacation. Your timeline is clear (2 years away), and his is vague ("summer or fall"). There’s no guarantee he’ll pay you back on time. 3. **Financial Responsibility**: You’ve already proven you can budget and save (despite living at home). His complaints about fairness ("you got more trips with parents") ignore the fact that *you* are actively planning for your own future, while he’s still relying on others for stability. 4. **Emotional Boundaries**: You’re uncomfortable with the idea of lending to him, and that’s valid. If he can’t respect your savings, there’s no reason to enable his poor financial habits. ### **Why It’s Still a Gray Area:** - **Family Dynamics**: Your parents’ involvement complicates things. They may expect you to help him, even if it’s not fair. If they pressure you, you might need to set firmer boundaries (e.g., "I can’t loan you money, but I’ll help you brainstorm ways to save"). - **His Argument Has Some Merit**: His point about fairness (e.g., you had more childhood trips, he had to work/college early) isn’t entirely baseless. However, his solution (taking *your* money) isn’t sustainable. A better approach might be for *both* of you to contribute to a shared fund for a future family trip, if that’s something you’re open to. - **Long-Term Trust**: If he keeps pushing, it could strain your relationship. You might need to say, "I care about you, but I can’t loan you money because I don’t trust you’ll pay me back." ### **What You Could Do Instead:** - **Offer Alternatives**: Suggest he save with you (e.g., "Let’s both put $X into a joint account for a future trip"). - **Set Conditions**: If you *do* lend him money, insist on a formal repayment plan (e.g., biweekly payments, collateral, or a penalty for late payments). - **Address the Root Issue**: His money struggles aren’t just about borrowing—they’re about responsibility. You could gently say, "I’m not lending you money, but if you want to go, start saving *yourself* like I did." ### **Final Verdict:** You’re **not** in the wrong for refusing, but the *how* you handle it matters. If you want to keep the peace, frame it as a boundary ("I can’t loan you money, but I’ll help you figure out how to save") rather than a rejection. If he keeps pushing, you may need to enforce consequences (e.g., no more family discussions about money). Would you like help drafting a response to him?
